english: for something to become urgent / for a deadline to be right on top of you (lit. 'fire falls on the top of your foot')
usage: 발등에 불 떨어져서 밤새 했어.
It got urgent at the last second, so I pulled an all-nighter.
Casual, explaining a scramble
마감이 코앞이라 이제 발등에 불 떨어졌어요.
The deadline's right there, so now it's crunch time.
Polite; pairs naturally with 코앞
발등에 불 떨어져야 움직이는 스타일이야.
I only get moving once it's down to the wire.
Describing a procrastinator habit
발등에 불이 떨어졌는데 아직도 시작을 안 했어?
It's crunch time and you still haven't started?
이/가 often added: 불이 떨어지다
examples: 서류 제출이 내일까지라 발등에 불 떨어졌어.
The documents are due tomorrow, so I'm in a last-minute panic.
Civic/paperwork scramble
발등에 불 떨어지고 나서야 부랴부랴 짐을 쌌어요.
Only when it became urgent did I hurriedly pack.
부랴부랴 = hurriedly, fits well
다들 발등에 불 떨어진 듯이 회의실로 뛰어갔어.
Everyone ran to the meeting room like it was an emergency.
Workplace urgency
nuance: Literally 'fire falls on the top of your foot' — when fire lands on your foot you jump instantly, so it means something has suddenly become urgent and you have to deal with it right now. It often carries a self-aware, procrastinator's tone ('I only act once it's an emergency'). Casual-to-polite, extremely common at work and around deadlines.
mistakes: Don't read it literally as a burn injury — it's about sudden urgency, not pain.
It's 발등 (top of the foot), not 발 — and 떨어지다 means 'falls,' so keep the whole phrase intact.

english: to be right around the corner / extremely close in time or distance (lit. 'it's right in front of your nose')
usage: 시험이 코앞이야, 큰일 났어.
The exam is right around the corner — I'm in trouble.
Casual, about looming time
마감이 코앞이라 정신없어요.
The deadline's right on top of us, so it's hectic.
Polite; very common with 마감
편의점 코앞인데 귀찮아서 안 나가.
The convenience store is right there but I'm too lazy to go.
Distance sense — 'a stone's throw'
코앞에 두고도 못 찾았어.
It was right under my nose and I still couldn't find it.
코앞에 두다 = to have right in front of you
examples: 이사 날짜가 코앞이라 짐 싸느라 바빠요.
Moving day is almost here, so I'm busy packing.
Imminent event
설날이 코앞인데 기차표를 아직 못 구했어.
Lunar New Year is around the corner and I still can't get a train ticket.
Seasonal urgency
회사가 집 코앞이라 걸어서 5분이면 가요.
The office is right by my place — five minutes on foot.
Short distance
nuance: Literally 'right in front of the nose,' 코앞 means something is extremely near — either in time (a deadline/event almost here) or in distance (a place very close by). Casual-to-polite and used constantly in daily life. With time it adds a sense of pressure ('no time left'); with distance it stresses how close and convenient something is.
mistakes: Write 코앞 as one word, not 코 앞.
Context decides whether it means 'soon' (time) or 'nearby' (distance) — don't assume only one.

english: to get chills down one's spine / be struck with fear or dread (lit. 'one's spine goes cold/shivery')
usage: 그 얘기 듣고 등골이 오싹했어.
I got chills down my spine hearing that.
Casual, fear/creepiness
밤에 혼자 그 길 걸으니까 등골이 오싹하더라고요.
Walking that road alone at night gave me the shivers.
Polite, recounting a creepy moment
사고 영상 보니까 등골이 다 오싹해.
Watching the accident footage sent a total chill down my spine.
다 adds 'completely'
생각만 해도 등골이 서늘해.
Just thinking about it sends a chill down my back.
등골이 서늘하다 = close variant
examples: 공포 영화에서 갑자기 소리가 나서 등골이 오싹했어요.
A sudden sound in the horror movie sent chills down my spine.
Horror/startle context
하마터면 큰일 날 뻔했다고 생각하니 등골이 오싹해.
Thinking I almost got into real trouble gives me the chills.
Dread over a close call
그 사람 눈빛이 너무 차가워서 등골이 오싹했어요.
His gaze was so cold it sent a shiver down my spine.
Unsettling person
nuance: 등골 is the line of your spine, and 오싹하다 is that sudden cold-shiver feeling, so together they describe chills running down your back from fear, dread, or creepiness. Use it for horror, scary stories, or the jolt of realizing you narrowly avoided disaster. Casual-to-polite. The near-synonym 등골이 서늘하다 ('spine goes cool') has the same chilling feel.
mistakes: It's about fear/dread chills, not feeling physically cold from weather.
Pair 등골 with 오싹하다 or 서늘하다 — don't swap in unrelated 춥다 ('cold').

english: to praise someone lavishly / can't stop praising (lit. 'the saliva in one's mouth dries up' — from talking so much)
usage: 엄마가 너 칭찬을 입에 침이 마르게 하더라.
Mom couldn't stop singing your praises.
Casual; usually 입에 침이 마르게 칭찬하다
사장님이 그 직원을 입에 침이 마르도록 칭찬하셨어요.
The boss praised that employee to no end.
Polite; 마르도록 is the common form
다들 그 식당을 입에 침이 마르게 추천해.
Everyone recommends that restaurant nonstop.
Extended to enthusiastic recommendations
입에 침이 마르게 자랑하던데 진짜 좋은가 봐.
They bragged about it endlessly, so it must be really good.
About relentless bragging
examples: 선생님이 네 그림을 입에 침이 마르게 칭찬하셨어.
The teacher praised your drawing to the skies.
Lavish praise
친구가 그 카페를 입에 침이 마르도록 얘기해서 가 봤어요.
My friend raved about that cafe so much that I went.
Praise leading to action
할머니는 손주 얘기만 나오면 입에 침이 마르게 칭찬하세요.
Grandma gushes nonstop whenever her grandkids come up.
Habitual gushing
nuance: Literally 'the saliva in the mouth dries up' — if you talk about how great something is long enough, your mouth runs dry, so it means to praise lavishly and tirelessly. Almost always used with 칭찬하다 ('praise'), 자랑하다 ('brag'), or 추천하다 ('recommend') in the form 입에 침이 마르게/마르도록. Casual-to-polite, warm tone.
mistakes: It means praising endlessly, not literally being thirsty or having a dry mouth.
Don't drop the verb — it's used as 입에 침이 마르게 + (칭찬하다/자랑하다), not on its own.

english: to work well together / be in sync as a team (lit. 'one's hands and feet match')
usage: 우리 둘은 손발이 잘 맞아.
The two of us work together really well.
Casual, about teamwork
새 팀이랑 손발이 맞아서 일이 수월해요.
I'm in sync with the new team, so work goes smoothly.
Polite, workplace
손발이 안 맞아서 자꾸 실수가 나.
We're out of sync, so mistakes keep happening.
손발이 안 맞다 = the opposite
오래 같이 일하니까 손발이 척척 맞네.
We've worked together so long we're perfectly in sync.
척척 = 'smoothly, snappily'
examples: 주방이랑 홀이 손발이 맞아야 장사가 잘돼요.
The kitchen and the floor have to be in sync for business to run well.
Restaurant teamwork
둘이 손발이 맞아서 행사를 무사히 끝냈어.
The two were in sync and pulled off the event without a hitch.
Successful collaboration
처음엔 손발이 안 맞았는데 이제 호흡이 잘 맞아요.
At first we were out of sync, but now we work in great harmony.
호흡이 맞다 is a close synonym
nuance: Literally 'hands and feet match,' it describes two or more people coordinating smoothly — their actions line up like a well-rehearsed team. It's about working rhythm and cooperation, not friendship. Casual-to-polite, very common at work and on any team. The opposite 손발이 안 맞다 means people keep getting in each other's way, and 호흡이 맞다 ('breathing matches') is a near-synonym.
mistakes: Use it for teamwork/coordination, not for romantic compatibility (that's 잘 어울리다 or 궁합이 맞다).
It needs two or more people — you can't be 손발이 맞다 by yourself.

english: to actively step up and help / throw oneself into something wholeheartedly (lit. 'to take off one's shoes and step forward')
usage: 네가 발 벗고 나서 줘서 진짜 고마워.
Thank you for stepping up and really pitching in.
Casual, expressing gratitude
이웃들이 발 벗고 나서서 도와줬어요.
The neighbors went out of their way to help.
Polite, about community help
회사가 발 벗고 나서서 문제를 해결했어.
The company actively stepped in and solved the problem.
Organization taking initiative
친구 일이라면 발 벗고 나서는 사람이야.
He's the type to drop everything to help a friend.
Describing a generous character
examples: 선배가 발 벗고 나서서 취업을 도와줬어요.
A senior went all in to help me find a job.
Going above and beyond
다들 발 벗고 나서서 이사를 도와줘서 금방 끝났어.
Everyone pitched in wholeheartedly with the move, so it finished fast.
Group effort
그 문제는 아무도 발 벗고 나서지 않아서 오래 방치됐어요.
Nobody stepped up for that issue, so it was left alone for ages.
Negative — no one took initiative
nuance: Literally 'to take off your shoes and step forward' — back when shoes were precious, taking them off to wade in showed you were ready to get fully involved, so it means to step up and help eagerly, not half-heartedly. It praises someone for taking initiative for others. Casual-to-polite, warm and approving. Spacing: 발 벗고 나서다 (three words).
mistakes: Mind the spacing: 발 벗고 나서다, not 발벗고 나서다.
It implies wholehearted, voluntary effort to help — don't use it for reluctant or forced help.

english: to feel the weight of responsibility / feel heavily burdened (lit. 'one's shoulders are heavy')
usage: 책임이 커서 어깨가 무거워.
The responsibility is big, so I feel the weight of it.
Casual, about pressure
중요한 일을 맡아서 어깨가 무겁습니다.
I've taken on an important task, so I feel the responsibility.
Polite/formal, common in work speeches
가장으로서 어깨가 무거워요.
As the breadwinner, I carry a heavy load.
About family responsibility
기대가 큰 만큼 어깨가 더 무거워.
The bigger the expectations, the heavier the burden.
Linking expectations to pressure
examples: 팀장이 되니까 어깨가 무거워졌어요.
Becoming team lead made the responsibility feel heavier.
New role
다들 나만 믿는다고 하니까 어깨가 무거워.
Everyone says they're counting on me, so I feel the weight.
Pressure from others' trust
큰 프로젝트를 혼자 맡아서 어깨가 너무 무거워요.
I'm handling a big project alone, so the burden feels heavy.
Heavy workload
nuance: Literally 'heavy shoulders,' it expresses the psychological weight of responsibility or expectation pressing down on you. It's a humble, common way to acknowledge that a duty feels serious — you'll hear it in acceptance speeches, new-role announcements, and everyday talk about pressure. Casual-to-polite/formal. The relief version is 어깨가 가벼워지다 ('shoulders get lighter').
mistakes: It's about emotional/responsibility burden, not literal shoulder pain or stiffness (that's 어깨가 결리다/아프다).
Don't confuse with 어깨가 처지다 ('shoulders droop'), which means feeling discouraged or dejected.

english: to be shameless / thick-skinned / have a lot of nerve (lit. 'one's face is thick')
usage: 걔 진짜 얼굴 두껍다, 또 부탁하네.
He's got some nerve — asking for a favor again.
Casual, mildly critical
그런 부탁을 하다니 얼굴이 두꺼우시네요.
Asking for that takes a lot of nerve.
Polite but pointed
나도 좀 얼굴 두꺼워져야 하나 봐.
Maybe I need to grow a thicker skin.
Self-talk — wishing to be less self-conscious
낯짝이 두꺼워서 미안한 줄을 몰라.
He's so brazen he doesn't even feel sorry.
낯짝/낯이 두껍다 = blunter variants
examples: 얼굴이 두꺼워서 거절을 당해도 또 시도해요.
He's thick-skinned, so even after a no he tries again.
Persistence read as shamelessness
그렇게 민폐 끼치고도 태연한 거 보면 얼굴 두껍다.
Causing all that trouble and staying calm — what nerve.
민폐 = being a nuisance
면접 땐 얼굴이 좀 두꺼워야 떨지 않아요.
For interviews you need a bit of thick skin so you don't get nervous.
Mildly positive 'don't be shy' sense
nuance: Literally 'thick face,' it means shameless or brazen — someone who isn't embarrassed when they should be. Usually mildly negative or teasing, though it can flip positive to mean 'not easily flustered' (e.g. for interviews or public speaking). Casual-to-polite. Blunter, harsher variants are 낯이 두껍다 and 낯짝이 두껍다, and the noun for the trait is 철면피.
mistakes: Nothing to do with literal skin thickness on the face — it's about shamelessness.
Tone matters: it can sound insulting, so don't say it bluntly to someone you must stay polite with.

english: to be incredibly busy / have no time to even breathe (lit. 'no moment to even open one's eyes and nose')
usage: 요즘 눈코 뜰 새 없이 바빠.
I'm so swamped these days I can't even catch a breath.
Casual; almost always with 바쁘다
연말이라 눈코 뜰 새 없이 지내고 있어요.
It's year-end, so I'm run off my feet.
Polite, about a hectic stretch
애 둘 키우느라 눈코 뜰 새가 없어.
Raising two kids leaves me no time to breathe.
새가 없다 form with 이/가
오픈 시간엔 눈코 뜰 새 없이 손님이 밀려와.
At opening time customers pour in nonstop.
Workplace rush
examples: 이사하고 정리하느라 눈코 뜰 새 없었어요.
I was swamped moving and unpacking.
Busy with a big task
행사 준비로 일주일 내내 눈코 뜰 새 없이 일했어.
I worked flat out all week preparing for the event.
Sustained busy period
식당이 점심엔 눈코 뜰 새 없이 바빠서 정신이 하나도 없어요.
The restaurant is so slammed at lunch I can't think straight.
Peak-hour chaos
nuance: Literally 'no gap to even open your eyes and nose,' it's a vivid way to say you're so busy you can't spare a second — busier than just 바쁘다. It's almost always used adverbially as 눈코 뜰 새 없이 바쁘다 ('busy without a moment to breathe'). Casual-to-polite, extremely common when describing a hectic stretch at work or home.
mistakes: Keep the spacing 눈코 뜰 새 없다 (눈코 is one word; 뜰 새 = 'a moment to open').
It's an intensity phrase usually attached to 바쁘다 — don't use it to mean simply 'I have no time' in a neutral way.

english: to get ripped off / be overcharged (lit. 'to wear a gourd dipper')
usage: 관광지에서 완전 바가지 썼어.
I got totally ripped off at the tourist spot.
Casual; 바가지(를) 쓰다 = the buyer overpays
택시 타다가 바가지 쓴 것 같아요.
I think I got overcharged in the taxi.
Polite, suspecting a ripoff
여기 비싸니까 바가지 쓰지 않게 가격 먼저 물어봐.
It's pricey here, so ask the price first to avoid getting fleeced.
Practical advice
사장이 외국인한테 바가지를 씌웠어.
The owner ripped the foreigner off.
바가지(를) 씌우다 = the seller does the overcharging
examples: 축제 음식이 평소의 두 배라 바가지 쓴 기분이었어요.
The festival food was double the usual price — felt like a ripoff.
Inflated event pricing
시세 모르고 샀다가 바가지 썼어.
I bought it without knowing the going rate and got overcharged.
시세 = market price
흥정 안 하면 시장에서 바가지 쓰기 쉬워요.
If you don't haggle you can easily get fleeced at the market.
흥정 = haggling, pairs naturally
nuance: Literally 'to wear a gourd dipper,' it means to be charged way more than something is worth — to get ripped off. Very common when talking about tourist traps, taxis, markets, and festivals. Casual-to-polite. Watch the pair: 바가지(를) 쓰다 = you (the buyer) overpay; 바가지(를) 씌우다 = the seller rips someone off. Often shortened to just 바가지.
mistakes: Don't reverse the verbs: 쓰다 = you got ripped off; 씌우다 = you (or the seller) ripped someone off.
It refers to being overcharged, not to a bad-quality product (that's just 별로다 / 안 좋다).

english: you won't get anything out of it / there'll be nothing in it for you (often a warning or threat) (lit. 'there's not even broth')
usage: 한 번만 더 늦으면 국물도 없어.
Be late one more time and you'll get nothing from me.
Casual warning/threat
약속 안 지키면 국물도 없을 줄 알아.
If you break the promise, don't expect anything good.
Half-joking threat among friends
이번에 도와줘도 나한테 국물도 없더라.
Even though I helped this time, I got nothing out of it.
Complaining about no payoff
그렇게 해 봤자 너한테 국물도 없어.
Even if you do that, there's nothing in it for you.
Pointing out a pointless effort
examples: 사장님이 또 실수하면 국물도 없다고 하셨어요.
The boss said if it happens again there'll be no mercy.
Workplace warning
내 말 안 들으면 다음부턴 국물도 없을 거야.
If you don't listen to me, next time you'll get nothing.
Parent/older-sibling tone
밤새 도왔는데 고맙단 말도 없고, 정말 국물도 없네.
I helped all night and didn't even get a thanks — nothing to show for it.
No reward at all
nuance: Literally 'not even broth (국물) left,' it means there's nothing to be gained — no benefit, leftover, or mercy. It's most often a half-joking warning or threat ('do that and you'll get nothing from me'), but can also describe an effort that paid off with zero reward. Casual register; the threat usage sounds blunt, so it's for friends, family, or clearly informal settings.
mistakes: Nothing to do with actual soup — 국물 here means 'leftover benefit/payoff.'
The threatening tone is informal and can sound harsh; don't use it in polite or professional contexts.

english: to throw cold water on something / ruin the mood or kill the momentum (lit. 'to pour cold water over')
usage: 분위기 좋았는데 걔가 찬물을 끼얹었어.
The mood was great but he threw cold water on it.
Casual, about a buzzkill
좋은 소식에 찬물을 끼얹고 싶진 않지만요.
I don't mean to rain on the good news, but…
Polite hedge before bad news
다들 신났는데 그 말 한마디가 찬물을 끼얹었어요.
Everyone was excited, but that one comment killed it.
A single remark ruining the mood
계획에 자꾸 찬물 끼얹지 말고 좀 응원해 줘.
Stop pouring cold water on the plan and cheer me on.
Asking someone to stop being negative
examples: 회의 분위기가 살아나려는데 부장님이 찬물을 끼얹었어요.
The meeting was warming up, but the manager threw cold water on it.
Workplace momentum killed
다 같이 여행 가자던 분위기에 한 명이 찬물을 끼얹었어.
Someone threw cold water on the whole let's-go-on-a-trip vibe.
Group plans deflated
축하 자리에 굳이 찬물을 끼얹는 말을 할 필요는 없잖아.
There's no need to say something that ruins a celebration.
Advising tact
nuance: Literally 'to pour cold water over (something hot),' it means to suddenly kill an upbeat mood, excitement, or momentum — usually with a negative comment or unwelcome news. Use it for the person or remark that deflates a good vibe. Casual-to-polite. It's close to 김(을) 빼다 / 김새다 ('to deflate excitement'), but 찬물을 끼얹다 stresses an active, deliberate buzzkill.
mistakes: Spelling: it's 끼얹다 (kki-eon-da), an easy verb to misspell — not 끼언다 or 끼엊다.
It implies actively spoiling a positive mood, so don't use it for just any bad news; there needs to be enthusiasm or momentum to ruin.
